lab_title: Vectors and Projectile Motion: From Components to Trajectories
top_level_objectives: Understand how vectors are represented as arrows with magnitude and direction, and how two vectors combine tip-to-tail to produce a resultant
Learn to decompose a single vector into horizontal and vertical components using trigonometry, and relate components back to magnitude and angle
Apply vector decomposition to the initial velocity of a projectile, recognizing that horizontal and vertical motions evolve independently
Predict and observe how changes in launch angle and speed alter a projectile's trajectory, range, and maximum height

scenes.scene_name: Vectors as Arrows: Magnitude and Direction
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce vectors as geometric objects with magnitude (length) and direction (angle), contrasting them with scalars and establishing visual intuition.
key_visuals: A large arrow emerging from the origin, with a labeled magnitude (length in meters) and direction angle (in degrees from horizontal)
A second arrow of different magnitude and direction appearing nearby, with similar labels
A pair of labeled axes (horizontal and vertical) with a protractor overlay to show angle measurement
Comparison boxes showing scalar (temperature: 25°C) vs. vector (velocity: 12 m/s at 35° above horizontal)
student_actions: Observe and identify the magnitude and direction of the displayed vectors
Use an interactive slider to adjust the angle of a vector and watch how its arrow rotates without changing its length
Use another slider to scale the magnitude while keeping direction fixed, observing how the arrow length changes
Answer a quick check: given a vector diagram, state whether a quantity is scalar or vector and explain why

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how two vectors combine geometrically to produce a resultant, building intuition for vector superposition.
key_visuals: First vector (e.g., 8 m/s northeast) drawn as a red arrow from a common origin
Second vector (e.g., 6 m/s east) drawn as a blue arrow starting from the tip of the first vector
Resultant vector drawn as a green arrow from the origin to the final tip, with its magnitude and direction labeled
Animation showing the vectors repositioning to illustrate the equivalence of different orderings (A+B = B+A)
student_actions: Watch the tip-to-tail combination unfold with narration explaining each step
Adjust the magnitude of the first vector using a slider and observe how the resultant changes
Adjust the direction of the second vector and observe the new resultant
Predict the approximate magnitude and direction of the resultant before it is calculated, then compare with the displayed result

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how a single vector can be broken into horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components, introducing the right-triangle relationship.
key_visuals: A vector at an arbitrary angle (e.g., 10 m/s at 40° above horizontal) drawn in a 2D coordinate system
Dashed perpendicular lines from the vector's tip dropping to the horizontal and vertical axes, forming a right triangle
Two component vectors (one along x-axis in red, one along y-axis in blue) with labeled magnitudes (e.g., vₓ = 7.7 m/s, vᵧ = 6.4 m/s)
The original vector drawn as the hypotenuse, with the right angle and angle θ clearly marked
student_actions: Observe how the right triangle emerges when a vector is decomposed
Drag the vector's endpoint to change its angle and magnitude, watching how the component values update dynamically
Use a trigonometry reference panel to confirm that vₓ = v·cos(θ) and vᵧ = v·sin(θ)
Check: use the Pythagorean theorem to verify that √(vₓ² + vᵧ²) returns the original magnitude

scenes.scene_name: From Components Back to Magnitude and Angle
scenes.brief_purpose: Reverse the decomposition process, emphasizing that magnitude and direction can be recovered from components using inverse trigonometry.
key_visuals: A horizontal component (red arrow labeled vₓ) and a vertical component (blue arrow labeled vᵧ) displayed separately
These two components then recombine tip-to-tail to show the resultant vector
Right triangle with sides vₓ and vᵧ, hypotenuse labeled as the magnitude v
Angle θ shown at the origin, with θ = arctan(vᵧ/vₓ) and v = √(vₓ² + vᵧ²) displayed
student_actions: Input or adjust values for vₓ and vᵧ using sliders
Observe the resulting vector magnitude and angle update in real time
Use the reference panel to verify the inverse trigonometric calculations
Solve a short problem: given vₓ and vᵧ, calculate v and θ, then check against the simulation's result

scenes.scene_name: Projectile Motion Setup: Decomposing Initial Velocity
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply vector decomposition to a projectile launched at an arbitrary angle, setting up the conceptual framework for independent horizontal and vertical motions.
key_visuals: A cannon or launcher positioned at ground level, angled at a selectable launch angle (θ)
An arrow representing the initial velocity vector emerging from the cannon's muzzle, with a given magnitude (e.g., 20 m/s)
Decomposition of this initial velocity into horizontal component (vₓ₀) and vertical component (vᵧ₀) with values displayed
A coordinate system overlay showing the launch position at the origin, with horizontal (x) and vertical (y) axes extending across a landscape
student_actions: Adjust the launch angle using a slider and observe how vₓ₀ and vᵧ₀ change
Adjust the initial speed and observe the effect on both components
Predict how the components will evolve during flight (e.g., will vₓ stay constant? Will vᵧ change?)
Answer conceptual questions: 'Why might horizontal and vertical motions be independent?'

scenes.scene_name: Independent Motions: Horizontal and Vertical Separately
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate that horizontal motion (constant velocity) and vertical motion (uniformly accelerated) are independent, allowing separate analysis.
key_visuals: A preview of the parabolic trajectory in faint gray
Vertical panel showing only the vertical component of velocity (vᵧ) as a function of time, starting at vᵧ₀ and decreasing linearly due to gravity (becoming negative after the apex)
Horizontal panel showing only the horizontal component of velocity (vₓ) remaining constant throughout the flight
A time slider that advances the simulation, updating both velocity panels and showing the projectile's position along both axes independently
Position graphs showing height (y) vs. time as a parabola, and horizontal displacement (x) vs. time as a line
student_actions: Play the animation and observe that vₓ remains constant while vᵧ decreases uniformly
Pause at various times and note the values of vₓ, vᵧ, x, and y
Verify that y = vᵧ₀·t - ½g·t² matches the observed vertical motion
Verify that x = vₓ₀·t matches the observed horizontal motion
Discuss: if only vertical motion were present (vₓ₀ = 0), what path would the projectile trace?

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how combining independent horizontal and vertical motions at each instant produces the characteristic parabolic trajectory.
key_visuals: A full parabolic trajectory drawn in a landscape scene with a launch point and landing zone
Real-time position marker on the trajectory, linked to the time slider, showing the projectile moving along the path
Velocity vector at the current position, decomposed into horizontal (red) and vertical (blue) components, updating continuously
Multiple snapshot positions and velocities along the arc, showing how the velocity vector rotates (becoming increasingly downward) as the projectile descends
Overlaid graphs showing x(t), y(t), vₓ(t), and vᵧ(t)
student_actions: Play the full animation and watch the projectile follow the parabolic path
Pause at the apex and observe that vᵧ = 0 at that moment, while vₓ remains nonzero
Pause during descent and observe that vᵧ has become negative, pointing downward
Compare the visual trajectory to the mathematical equation y = (tan θ)·x - (g/(2v₀²·cos²θ))·x²
Identify the vertex (apex) and range (horizontal distance at landing)

scenes.scene_name: Exploring Angle and Speed: How They Shape the Trajectory
scenes.brief_purpose: Allow students to manipulate launch angle and initial speed, observing how these parameters affect range, maximum height, and trajectory shape.
key_visuals: A launcher with adjustable angle (slider from 0° to 90°) and adjustable initial speed (slider from 0 to 50 m/s)
A landscape with multiple parabolic trajectories displayed simultaneously (e.g., at angles 30°, 45°, 60°, all at the same speed) for comparison
Real-time displays of range, maximum height, and time of flight for the current trajectory
Animation showing how trajectory shape changes as angle or speed is adjusted
student_actions: Set the speed to a fixed value (e.g., 20 m/s) and vary the angle from 0° to 90°, noting which angle produces the maximum range
Verify that 45° yields the maximum range (neglecting air resistance)
Set the angle to 30° and to 60°, and observe that both produce the same range but different maximum heights and flight times
Increase the initial speed while keeping the angle fixed, and observe that range increases quadratically
Answer synthesis questions: 'What angle maximizes height for a given speed? What angle is optimal for a long horizontal throw?'
Predict the trajectory before running the simulation, then compare prediction with result
